common_name: Old Heavy Berry American Holly (Exceptionally Fruitful Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container trees in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Old Heavy Berry is a female selection valued specifically for unusually heavy annual berry production. Plant a compatible male American holly within range for fruit set.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a compatible male American holly within range for pollination, since hollies are dioecious and only fertilized female plants set berries. Old Heavy Berry, one of the longest-cultivated named American holly selections, is prized for producing an unusually dense, reliable crop of bright red berries nearly every year, holding its fruit through much of winter as a valuable food source for cedar waxwings, robins, and other birds during the leanest part of the season. Its glossy, spiny, dark evergreen foliage forms a dense pyramidal tree that works well as a specimen, screen, or wildlife planting in acidic-soil landscapes across its native range. It grows slowly but steadily and needs only occasional shaping to maintain a full, well-proportioned form.

common_name: Henry Hicks Sweetbay Magnolia (Evergreen Cold-Hardy Sweetbay)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Henry Hicks is selected for reliably evergreen foliage and good cold hardiness compared to seedling sweetbay, which can be deciduous or semi-evergreen depending on provenance.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; sweetbay magnolia tolerates wetter, boggier soil than most magnolias. Henry Hicks was selected specifically for holding its glossy, dark green, silver-backed leaves through winter more reliably than typical seedling-grown sweetbay, which often loses its leaves or looks ragged in cold weather, while also showing better cold hardiness than many evergreen selections. Creamy-white, lemon-scented flowers open through the summer, providing a long season of fragrance and pollinator value, and the tree supports Promethea silk moth and tiger swallowtail caterpillars as a larval host. Its narrow, upright form and tolerance of wet soil make it a strong choice for a rain garden, pond edge, or naturalistic planting where a reliably evergreen native tree is wanted.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba does not transplant well when large, so choose a small container tree and disturb roots as little as possible.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Alba is a classic, long-cultivated white-flowered selection of eastern redbud, covering its bare branches in pure white, pea-like flowers in early spring before the heart-shaped green leaves emerge, a striking contrast to the more familiar rosy-pink flowered species and useful for gardeners who want the redbud form and season without the pink flower color. It grows into the same small, often multi-trunked tree with an attractive horizontal branching habit as straight-species redbud, providing dappled shade in summer and yellow fall color before leaf drop. Plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are prone to rot in poorly drained, consistently wet sites, and give it some afternoon shade in the hottest part of zone 9 to reduce summer leaf stress.

common_name: Cherokee Chief Dogwood (Deep Red-Bracted Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in dappled light with cool, moist, acidic soil; Cherokee Chief is one of the most widely planted red-bracted flowering dogwood cultivars, from the same North Carolina breeding line as the white-bracted Cherokee Princess.

directions: Cherokee Chief is one of the most widely planted deep-red-bracted flowering dogwood cultivars, opening rich rose-red bracts in early spring on bare branches before the leaves emerge, a bold contrast to the classic white-bracted straight species. Plant in moist, acidic, organically rich soil in partial shade, protecting it from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, both of which stress flowering dogwood and increase susceptibility to powdery mildew and other foliar problems. Mulch to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist, since dogwood roots are sensitive to both drought and waterlogging. Red fall foliage and berry-like fruit that feeds birds follow the spring bloom; prune only lightly right after flowering to maintain the tree's naturally tiered, horizontal branching structure.
